transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Rivervue Head of ML), Daniel Ortiz (Platform Eng), Priya Rao (Security), Tom Ellis (CTO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time. we're Maya from Redwood, with Samir, our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:06] Laura Kim: Good thanks, Maya. Appreciate you fitting us in. Quick note we got a lot to cover so maybe we start with our production constraints.
[00:12] Tom Ellis: Yep, quick background — we run a mix of real-time fraud scoring and a customer conversational assistant; both are latency sensitive but different patterns. Fraud is many small requests sub 200ms target, assistant is bursty with longer token outputs.
[00:25] Samir Patel: Thanks, that's helpful. Can you say a bit about qps, tails and any average token lengths you see?
[00:32] Daniel Ortiz: Sure, average queries per second for fraud endpoint is about 45 sustained with peaks to 250 for a few minutes during settlement windows. Typical token outputs are small, like 8-16 tokens. Conversational assistant is more like 10 sustained and spikes to 120 with outputs 100-400 tokens.
[00:48] Laura Kim: We also have strict isolation requirements for PCI-adjacent data. We can't have multi-tenant noisy neighbors and we need audit logs + key separation.
[00:56] Priya Rao: Yes and we prefer a private deployment or dedicated capacity - basically reserved GPUs within Redwood. We need to understand encryption at rest, KMS/HSM integration and SSO provisioning.
[01:06] Maya Chen: Totally understood. So Dedicated from Redwood maps well there — reserved GPU pools, VPC peering options, and customer-level KMS integrations. There are a couple of levers: you can reserve capacity for baseline throughput and have burstable headroom, or go for a bigger fixed pool. Both have tradeoffs.
[01:20] Tom Ellis: Can you explain burstable headroom? Is that on the same hardware or does it spill to hosted? We're concerned about data routing to shared infra.
[01:28] Samir Patel: Good question. We offer two patterns: 1) Dedicated pool with reserved baseline and an optional burst overlay that's still within your dedicated tenancy but billed differently — think pre-warmed GPUs you can spin up quickly within your reservation footprint. 2) Failover to compatible hosted variants in emergency, which is never used for PCI data unless you opt in and sign a data flow agreement. There's sometimes a mis- — sorry mishtype — miscommunication where folks assume hosted = data leaks; with Redwood we can keep burst inside your dedicated boundary.
[01:56] Daniel Ortiz: Ok that second option is critical. Our SecOps won't allow routing to hosted without heavy signoff.
[02:02] Priya Rao: We need to see the network topology diagrams and audit log examples. Also SLAs on latency and GPU isolation guarantees.
[02:10] Maya Chen: We'll share the security pack and a dedicated architecture diagram. For SLAs, Dedicated comes with uptime and latency SLOs on the pool, and we can bake in a redundancy strategy across AZs or regions for critical endpoints.
[02:22] Laura Kim: What's Redwood's typical lead time for provisioning a dedicated pool for a new customer?
[02:27] Samir Patel: Typical is 2-4 weeks for standard configurations. Private/on-prem installs take longer — usually 6-12 weeks depending on approvals and network setup. If you need faster, we can pre-stage quotas in region.
[02:39] Tom Ellis: Cost — how should we think about reserved vs on-demand? Our finops team will push back on idle GPUs.
[02:45] Maya Chen: There are a few cost models: monthly reserved (committed) with a lower unit price, and a burst top-up rate. Many customers model a baseline to cover 90% of typical load and use burst for short peaks. Our Optimize tooling can simulate cost for your traffic profile once Samir has the histograms.
[03:01] Daniel Ortiz: That optimize tool — does it recommend quantization or batching heuristics? We use mixed precision for some models and want to understand memory/cost tradeoffs.
[03:09] Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood Optimize suggests quantization levels, batching thresholds, and cache strategies — for example prefix KV caching for conversational flows to reduce work per-token. On dedicated we can give config recommendations and apply kernel/compilation profiles that improve throughput.
[03:25] Laura Kim: On models — we run a mix of open models (Llama variants, Mistral-like stuff) and a few finetuned proprietary checkpoints. Are there constraints on bringing your own model to Dedicated?
[03:35] Samir Patel: You can bring custom models; we do model onboarding to validate compilation/compatibility and we recommend a short validation run. For proprietary checkpoints we support encrypted model storage and customer-controlled keys if you want.
[03:45] Tom Ellis: What about scaling during extreme spikes like subpoenaed activity or marketing events — minutes to scale?
[03:52] Samir Patel: Scaling ramp time depends on region capacity and reserved headroom. If you pre-commit to a burst buffer (the pre-warmed overlay), scaling can be a matter of 30-90 seconds to attach more GPUs to the pool. If you rely on region capacity without pre-warm, it can be several minutes and depends on overall cluster utilization.
[04:08] Laura Kim: 30-90 seconds sounds good. Do you have numbers on tail latencies under sustained load? For fraud we need p95 < 200ms.
[04:16] Samir Patel: We'd want to run a benchmark with your real prompts. In our experience on similarly sized pools, p95 for small token outputs can be sub-200ms with continuous batching off and low queueing. But benchmarks vary a lot — we'll run a one-week perf plan to measure.
[04:30] Daniel Ortiz: Ok let's talk observability — we need token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and traces for troubleshooting.
[04:36] Maya Chen: Redwood Console exposes per-route dashboards, token cost, traces, and retention policies. For Dedicated we can extend retention or ship logs to your S3 or logging endpoint for audit.
[04:48] Priya Rao: How do you handle key rotations and HSM integration? Our policy requires quarterly rotation and centralized KMS logs.
[04:55] Samir Patel: We integrate with customer KMS providers via customer-controlled keys. Key rotation is supported, and audit logs are exported. For HSM-backed keys we can support via partner integrations; we'll include the exact flow in the security docs.
[05:08] Tom Ellis: Are there any hard limits on GPU types? We want A100s for throughput, but also some cheaper RTX-style or L4s for embed workloads.
[05:16] Samir Patel: Customers can choose GPU flavors in Dedicated. A100 or H100 for heavy models and L4/A10 for embeddings or lower-cost inference. You can mix pools by workload type — e.g., fraud on A100, embeddings on L4.
[05:28] Laura Kim: How do you manage model variants for fallback? If we quantize for cost, we need a policy to fall back to FP16 if quality regresses.
[05:36] Maya Chen: We support rollout policies and automatic fallback based on quality/regression signals. Redwood Optimize will flag regressions for your test prompts and you can do canary rollouts across pools.
[05:46] Daniel Ortiz: Let's cover integration timeline. If we sign a reserved contract, what are typical milestones?
[05:52] Samir Patel: Typical: week 0 sign, week 1 kickoff and network config, week 2 provisioning and model onboarding, week 3 internal smoke tests, week 4 production cutover — so 2-4 weeks end to end for most customers. Private/on-prem adds extra lead time.
[06:08] Priya Rao: We also need to run a security review; can we get the SOC2, penetration test results and a data flow diagram?
[06:14] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll attach the SOC2 report, recent pentest summary and an architecture diagram showing VPC peering and audit log flows.
[06:22] Laura Kim: A couple of detailed questions from platform: 1) how is KV cache persisted across replicas? 2) how do you handle stateful convos if nodes fail?
[06:31] Samir Patel: Good ones. KV cache is stored in a local in-memory cache for hot paths with optional TTL-based warmers; for dedicated we can enable a shared cache layer that is replicated across availability zones. Stateful conversations can either use session affinity to a node or be reconstructed via the KV cache; fallback strategies are documented. There's a tradeoff between latency and consistency which we can tune.
[06:52] Daniel Ortiz: Session affinity worries us a bit for scale. Are sticky sessions supported at the load balancer level?
[06:58] Samir Patel: Yes, we support session affinity and sticky routing at the request router; for high-availability you can combine affinity with replicated caches.
[07:06] Tom Ellis: Our compliance requires logs ingested to our GCP project, not third-party buckets. Can Redwood push logs directly?
[07:12] Maya Chen: We can push logs to your cloud bucket (GCP/AWS) over private peering. We'll include delivery options in the security pack.
[07:21] Laura Kim: On failover: if an AZ becomes unavailable, what's the RTO for recovering GPU capacity?
[07:27] Samir Patel: If you have cross-AZ redundancy configured, RTOs are generally under 5 minutes for routing and attaching spare instances. If you require cross-region failover, that's longer and we recommend active-active or warm-standby setups.
[07:39] Priya Rao: Anything about data residency for EU customers? We have EU users, but primary is US. We may later need EU-only tenancy.
[07:47] Maya Chen: We support region-specific deployments and can ensure model hosting and logs remain in-region for EU-only tenancy.
[07:53] Laura Kim: Ok practical next steps — you mentioned a benchmark. What do you need from us?
[07:58] Samir Patel: We'll need representative prompts, a 7-day traffic histogram, sample payload sizes, and sample models/checkpoints to run the test. Also target SLOs for p95/p99 latency and budget constraints.
[08:10] Daniel Ortiz: We'll assemble that. One more thing — can you share an example pricing scenario with baseline + burst costs for our profile?
[08:18] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share a pricing scenario and a cost simulator output based on the histograms.
[08:24] Tom Ellis: Any legal caveats in the standard dedicated contract about data use? We can't have models trained on our data.
[08:31] Maya Chen: Redwood's standard language for Dedicated says we don't use customer data for model training unless explicitly contracted. We'll flag the clause for legal.
[08:38] (cross-talk)
[08:40] Priya Rao: Small point — can user-level access be enforced via SSO + RBAC? Our teams need least-privilege.
[08:45] Samir Patel: Yes SAML/SSO + RBAC and token scoping for per-route access are supported.
[08:50] Maya Chen: Great, I think we've got clear asks. Samir, do you want to summarize the technical / benchmark plan?
[08:55] Samir Patel: Sure. We'll propose a one-week benchmark: day 0 onboarding + model validation, days 1-5 run synthetic and replayed traffic for fraud and assistant endpoints, collect p50/p95/p99, token cost, and resource utilization. We'll compare A100 vs L4 configs for cost/latency tradeoffs, and run a small quantization experiment. We need the prompt sets, sample models, and traffic histograms.
[09:18] Laura Kim: Sounds good. We'll prioritize sending prompts and histograms.
[09:22] Maya Chen: I'll send the pricing deck and security pack after the call. I'll also include a draft PO/contract timeline.
[09:29] Tom Ellis: End state — if benchmarks look good we'll aim to sign reserved capacity for the fraud workload first and then expand for assistant. That align with your recommended approach?
[09:36] Maya Chen: That's a common pattern and it works well. Start with the most latency-sensitive workload as the baseline.
[09:40] (break)
[09:42] Maya Chen: Any final questions?
[09:44] Priya Rao: No, thanks. Please mark the SOC2 doc as part of the deliverables.
[09:48] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone for your time. We'll follow up with the docs and the benchmark plan.
[09:54] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcription with occasional mis-attributions and minor word errors (e.g., "mishtype" for mis-communication). Some technical terms abbreviated (KV, KMS, SLO).
